source.title: A positive proportion of locally soluble hyperelliptic curves over Q have no point over any odd degree extension
source.authors: Manjul Bhargava, Benedict H. Gross and Xiaoheng Wang (appendix by Tim and Vladimir Dokchitser)
source.venue: Journal of the American Mathematical Society 30 (2017), 451–493
readSections: The entire arXiv v2 (24 February 2017, dated March 2, 2017; 42 pages; §§1–12, Appendix A and references), read 2026-09-22. PDF from arxiv.org, SHA-256 8833a226eea99eab7e48b90de7d747fa535eafe032d5c62fd50812d38ad4c4f2. The JAMS version (online 27 July 2016) returned 403 to scripted access; v2 postdates it and is presumably the final text. Locators are v2 pages.

items.name: Hyperelliptic curves z² = f(x, y) ordered by height
items.statement: A hyperelliptic curve C over Q of genus g ≥ 1 is a smooth geometrically irreducible complete curve with a degree-2 map to P¹; it is z² = f(x, y) = f_0x^n + ⋯ + f_ny^n in P(1, 1, g + 1), n = 2g + 2, with f_i ∈ Z and Δ(f) ≠ 0. H(C) := H(f) := max|f_i| (2). C is locally soluble if C(Q_ν) ≠ ∅ for every place ν; more than 75% of curves are ([27], [3]).
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.0 as a source.

items.name: The Jacobian J = Pic⁰ and the torsor J¹ = Pic¹
items.statement: J = Pic⁰_{C/Q} is the Jacobian and J¹ = Pic¹_{C/Q} the J-torsor of degree-one divisor classes; d is the hyperelliptic class (pull-back of O(1)), and Pic_{C/K}/Z·d = J ⊔ J¹. A point of C over an extension of odd degree k gives the rational point (sum of conjugates) − ((k − 1)/2)d of J¹.
items.note: SF.3 plans Picard schemes and Jacobians (integrating AlgebraicCurves and JacobianChallenge).

items.name: Two-covers, the class W[2] and the 2-Selmer group
items.statement: A two-cover of a J-torsor I is an unramified π : Y → I with Y a J-torsor and π(y + a) = π(y) + 2a (degree 2^{2g}); its isomorphism class is the class of Y[2] in H¹(Q, J[2]). Locally soluble two-covers of J form Sel_2(J), with 0 → J(Q)/2J(Q) → Sel_2(J) → Ш_J[2] → 0. The two-cover J¹ →(×2) J² ≅ J gives W[2] ∈ Sel_2(J) when C is locally soluble, and W[2] maps to 0 in Ш_J[2] iff J¹(Q) ≠ ∅.
items.note: Routed to HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions RP.1/RP.3 as a source.

items.name: W[2] and odd factorizations
items.statement: The points of W[2] are the Weierstrass divisors e of degree 1 with 2e ≡ d, and correspond to the odd factorizations f = gh of f over Q (g, h of odd degree, rational or conjugate over a quadratic field). So W[2] ≠ 0 whenever f has no odd factorization, which by Hilbert irreducibility is 100% of the time.
items.note: Routed to HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions RP.1/RP.3 as a source.

items.name: The 2-Selmer set Sel_2(J¹) and the 2-Selmer set of order k
items.statement: Sel_2(J¹) is the set of isomorphism classes of locally soluble two-covers of J¹. It is empty or a principal homogeneous space for Sel_2(J), and equals the set of elements of Sel_4(J) mapping to W[2]. For odd k > 0, the 2-Selmer set of order k is the subset of classes that come locally at every ν from points e_ν − ((k − 1)/2)d with e_ν an effective Q_ν-divisor of degree k.
items.note: Routed to HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions RP.1/RP.3 as a source.

items.name: Hilbert irreducibility: odd and even factorizations are rare
items.statement: For 100% of integral binary forms of degree n ordered by height, f has no odd or even factorization over Q, so W[2] ≠ 0 and J(Q)[2] = 0.
items.note: IG.2 plans Hilbert irreducibility.

items.name: Remark 4 (J¹(Q) is empty or infinite)
items.statement: For 100% of locally soluble hyperelliptic curves over Q, J¹(Q) is either empty or infinite: if J¹(Q) ≠ ∅ then W[2] lies in the image of J(Q)/2J(Q), and since W[2] ≠ 0 and J(Q)[2] = 0, J(Q) has positive rank.
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 5 (Sel_2(J¹) is empty for a positive proportion)
items.statement: Fix g ≥ 1. For a positive proportion of locally soluble hyperelliptic curves C over Q of genus g, Sel_2(J¹) = ∅. Proof: if Sel_2(J¹) ≠ ∅, then #Sel_2(J¹) = #Sel_2(J) ≥ 2, and ≥ 4 when rk_2 Sel_2(J) is even; combine Theorem 6 (average ≤ 2) with the appendix (a positive proportion have even 2-Selmer rank).
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 6 (the average size of Sel_2(J¹) is at most 2)
items.statement: Fix g ≥ 1. When locally soluble hyperelliptic curves over Q of genus g are ordered by height, the average size of Sel_2(J¹) is at most 2 (expected to equal 2). The same holds over any large congruence family with locally soluble Div¹ (§12).
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorems 1, 2 and 12 (no points over odd-degree extensions; index 2)
items.statement: Fix g ≥ 1. For a positive proportion of locally soluble hyperelliptic curves C over Q of genus g: C has no point over any odd-degree extension of Q (Theorem 1); equivalently J¹(Q) = ∅ (Theorem 2); equivalently the index I(C), the gcd of degrees of rational divisors, is 2 (Theorem 12). These follow from Theorem 5.
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Corollary 3 (nontrivial 2-torsion in Ш)
items.statement: Fix g ≥ 1. A positive proportion of locally soluble hyperelliptic curves over Q of genus g have nontrivial 2-torsion in the Tate–Shafarevich group of their Jacobian (the image of W[2]).
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 7 and Corollary 8 (Selmer sets of order k)
items.statement: Fix an odd k > 0. The average size of the 2-Selmer set of order k over locally soluble hyperelliptic curves of genus g is < 2 if k < g, and tends to 0 as g → ∞. Hence for fixed m > 0, as g → ∞, 100% of hyperelliptic curves of genus g have no points over any extension of Q of odd degree ≤ m (Corollary 8). Proof at ∞: with 2m real roots, the image of Sym^k(C)(R) in J¹(R)/2J(R) (of size 2^{m−1}) has at most S_m(k) = C(m, 1) + C(m, 3) + ⋯ + C(m, k) elements, and S_{g+1}(k) < 2^g for k < g; for g → ∞ use Dembo–Poonen–Shao–Zeitouni.
items.locator: Theorem 7, Corollary 8, p.3; proof §12, pp.33–34, arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Dembo–Poonen–Shao–Zeitouni: random polynomials have many real roots
items.statement: The density of real polynomials of degree n with fewer than log n/log log n real roots is O(n^{−b+o(1)}) for some b > 0 ([15, Theorem 1.2]).
items.locator: Proof of Theorem 7, p.34, citing [15], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Skorobogatov–Stoll: the two-cover descent obstruction is Brauer–Manin
items.statement: The non-existence of a locally soluble two-cover of J¹ is a Brauer–Manin obstruction, both for J¹ and for Sym^k(C) (Skorobogatov [33, Theorem 6.1.1]; Stoll [34, Remark 6.5, Theorem 7.1]; via Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc descent).
items.note: RP.3 plans torsor descent and its comparison with Brauer–Manin under the chosen hypotheses.

items.name: Corollary 9 and Theorems 10–11 (Hasse principle failures with a Brauer–Manin obstruction)
items.statement: For fixed odd k > 0, as g → ∞, Sym^k(C) fails the Hasse principle for a proportion approaching 100% of locally soluble hyperelliptic C over Q of genus g, and the failure is a Brauer–Manin obstruction (Corollary 9, Theorem 11). For fixed g ≥ 1, for a positive proportion of locally soluble C, the g-dimensional variety J¹ has a Brauer–Manin obstruction to a rational point (Theorem 10).
items.note: Routed to HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions RP.1/RP.3 as a source.

items.name: The representation 2 ⊗ Sym²(n) over a Dedekind domain
items.statement: For a Dedekind domain D (quotient field K, char ≠ 2) and n ≥ 2, SL_n(D) acts on pairs (A, B) of symmetric bilinear forms on D^n. The invariant form f(x, y) = disc(xA − yB) := (−1)^{n(n−1)/2}det(xA − yB) = f_0x^n + ⋯ + f_ny^n has n + 1 coefficients, of degree n, which freely generate the invariants. Δ(f) has degree 2n(n − 1) in the entries. For even n, μ_2 acts trivially and (SL_n/μ_2)(D) acts, with 1 → SL_n(D)/μ_2(D) → (SL_n/μ_2)(D) → H¹(D, μ_2) → 1 and 1 → D^×/D^{×2} → H¹(D, μ_2) → Pic(D)[2] → 1.
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: The order R_f and the ideals I(k)
items.statement: For f_0 ≠ 0, f(x, 1) = f_0g(x), L = K[x]/g(x), θ the image of x, ζ_k = f_0θ^k + ⋯ + f_{k−1}θ. R = R_f = ⟨1, ζ_1, …, ζ_{n−1}⟩_D is an order of discriminant Δ(f). I(k) = ⟨1, θ, …, θ^k, ζ_{k+1}, …, ζ_{n−1}⟩ are fractional ideals with I(k) = I(1)^k, and (1/f′(θ))I(n − 2) is the trace dual of R ([9], [25, Proposition 1.1], [39, §2.1]).
items.note: The ring R_f is also an item of PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-25 (ST.1); coalesce. Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 16 (SL_n(D)-orbits and triples (I, α, s); after Wood)
items.statement: For f over D with Δ(f), f_0 ≠ 0, SL_n(D)-orbits with invariant form f are in bijection with equivalence classes of triples (I, α, s): I a fractional R-ideal, α ∈ L^×, s ∈ K^×, with I² ⊂ αI(n − 3), N(I) = sD and N(α) = s²f_0^{n−3}; (I, α, s) ~ (cI, c²α, N(c)s). The stabilizer is S^×[2]_{N=1}, S = End_R(I). The forms are λ, μ ↦ the ζ_{n−1}- and ζ_{n−2}-coefficients of λμ/α in I(n − 3) ([40, Theorem 1.3]).
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 17 and Remark 18 ((SL_n/μ_2)(D)-orbits)
items.statement: For even n, (SL_n/μ_2)(D)-orbits with invariant form f are in bijection with triples (I, α, s) up to (cMI, c²tα, N(c)t^{n/2}s), c ∈ L^×, t ∈ K^×(2) with tD = M²; stabilizers contain S^×[2]_{N=1}/D^×[2]. If D is a PID and every fractional R-ideal is principal, the classes are (R^×/R^{×2}D^×)_{N=f_0}, and the stabilizer is (R^×[2])_{N=1}/D^×[2] for n ≡ 2 mod 4, and an extension (3) for n ≡ 0 mod 4.
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Corollaries 19–20 (orbits over a field)
items.statement: Over a field K: SL_n(K)-orbits with invariant f correspond to pairs (α, s) with N(α) = s²f_0^{n−3} modulo (c²α, N(c)s), with stabilizer (Res_{L/K}μ_2)_{N=1}; for even n, (SL_n/μ_2)(K)-orbits correspond to pairs modulo (c²tα, N(c)t^{n/2}s), t ∈ K^×, with stabilizer (Res_{L/K}μ_2)_{N=1}/μ_2 ([6, Theorems 7–8]). So the orbit set maps bijectively or 2-to-1 to (L^×/L^{×2}K^×)_{N=f_0} according as f has an odd factorization or not. Stabilizer elements are even factorizations.
items.locator: Corollaries 19–20 and the following paragraphs, pp.8–9, citing [6], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Kummer theory: H¹(K, μ_2) = K^×/K^{×2}
items.statement: For a field K of characteristic ≠ 2, the Kummer map identifies K^×/K^{×2} with H¹(K, μ_2).
items.note: Corrected by REV-PAPER-BHARGAVA-GROSS-WANG-17 from library to planned. The libraries have the injection only: TauCeti.kummerClassMap_injective (TauCeti/FieldTheory/GaloisCohomology/Kummer.lean:298 at f790474) gives Kˣ/(Kˣ)ⁿ ↪ H¹(G_K, μₙ), and its own docstring says that surjectivity, which needs Hilbert 90, is what would upgrade it to the Kummer isomorphism; Mathlib's groupCohomology.isMulCoboundary₁_of_isMulCocycle₁_of_aut_to_units (RepresentationTheory/Homological/GroupCohomology/Hilbert90.lean:84 at 082e2d3) is the finite-Galois Hilbert 90, not the profinite statement the surjectivity needs. The paper uses the identification itself, printing 'H¹(K, μ_2) = K^×/K^{×2}' on p.8. The Tau Ceti ProfiniteCohomology roadmap, Layer 9, plans exactly this: Hilbert 90 for G_K and then the Kummer sequence and isomorphism.

items.name: The singular curve C_m and its generalized Jacobian J_m
items.statement: For f_0 ≠ 0, let P, P′ be the points of C above ∞ (rational over K′ = K(√f_0)), m = P + P′, and C_m : z² = f(x, y)y² the curve with an ordinary double point Q at ∞ ([30, Ch. IV, §4]). J_m = Pic⁰_{C_m} fits into 0 → T → J_m → J → 0 (5), with T the one-dimensional torus split by K′. Pic_{C_m}/Z·d = J_m ⊔ J¹_m, and there are morphisms C → J¹ and C − {P, P′} → J¹_m.
items.note: Routed to NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties R11.4 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 21 (rational divisor classes versus rational divisors)
items.statement: Pic_{C/K}(K)/Pic(C/K) ↪ Br(K′/K) = K^×/N(K′^×) (quaternion algebras split by K′). Hence if C has a rational divisor of odd degree, every K-rational divisor class is represented by a K-rational divisor; over a global field the same holds if Div¹(C) is locally soluble.
items.locator: Proposition 21 and the preceding paragraph, p.10; §3, p.11, arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Mathlib 082e2d3 has the Brauer group (Algebra/BrauerGroup/Defs.lean), but not this injection. Routed to SchemeAndStackFoundations SF.3 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 22 (2-torsion of J_m and J and the torsors W_m[2], W[2])
items.statement: With L = K[x]/f(x, 1): J_m[2] ≅ (Res_{L/K}μ_2)_{N=1}, whose K-points are the even-degree factors of f over K; J[2] ≅ (Res_{L/K}μ_2)_{N=1}/μ_2, whose K-points are the even factorizations; W_m[2] ⊂ J¹_m and W[2] ⊂ J¹ are torsors whose K-points are the odd-degree factors, resp. the odd factorizations. The Weil pairing makes J[2] self-dual, and H¹(K, J[2]) → H²(K, μ_2) is cup product with W[2] ([28, Proposition 10.3]).
items.locator: Proposition 22 and proof, pp.11–12, citing [22], [28], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties R11.4 as a source.

items.name: Generic pencils and their Fano schemes
items.statement: For symmetric A, B on W = K^n, the pencil is generic if Δ(disc(xA − yB)) ≠ 0, i.e. the base locus Y is a smooth complete intersection of dimension n − 3. The Fano scheme F(A, B) is the Hilbert scheme of maximal linear subspaces in Y. For n = 2g + 1 it is a finite torsor for (Res_{L/K}μ_2)_{N=1}. For n = 2g + 2 it is a smooth g-dimensional torsor for J, whose points are the g-dimensional subspaces isotropic for the whole pencil ([37]).
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 23 (Wang: the group J ⊔ F ⊔ J¹ ⊔ F)
items.statement: For a generic pencil with invariant form f and n = 2g + 2, X := J ⊔ F ⊔ J¹ ⊔ F has a commutative algebraic group structure over K, so [F] ∈ H¹(K, J) is 4-torsion with 2[F] = [J¹]. Multiplication by 2 gives two-covers F → J¹ and F[4] → W[2]. So the classes of J¹ in H¹(K, J) and of W[2] in H¹(K, J[4]) must be divisible by 2. This necessary condition is not sufficient, as z² = −x² − y² over R shows ([37, Theorem 2.7]).
items.locator: Theorem 23 and the following paragraphs, pp.12–13, citing [37], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Regular pencils: (A′, B′) = (A ⊕ ⟨aa′⟩, B ⊕ ⟨ab′ + a′b⟩)
items.statement: On W ⊕ K², (A′, B′) has invariant form f(x, y)y², a base locus with one ordinary double point, and 2g + 3 singular quadrics, all simple cones. Its algebra L′ ≅ L ⊕ K[y]/y², and W ⊕ K² is free of rank 1 over it. The Fano scheme F_m of (g + 1)-planes isotropic for the pencil and not containing the radical line of A′ is a smooth non-projective J_m-torsor. X_m = J_m ⊔ F_m ⊔ J¹_m ⊔ F_m is a group (7) with 2[F_m] = [J¹_m].
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 24 and Theorem 13 (when is f the discriminant of a pencil?)
items.locator: Theorem 13, p.5; Theorem 24 and proof, pp.14–15, arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 25, Proposition 26 and Lemma 27 (the obstruction classes coincide)
items.statement: The obstruction classes for conditions (a)–(h) are all equal in H²(K, J_m[2]): [f_0] = δ[J¹_m]. [f_0] comes from K^×/(K^{×2}N(L^×)) ↪ H²(K, (Res_{L/K}μ_2)_{N=1}), and δ is the connecting map of 0 → J_m[2] → J_m → J_m → 0. Proof: for a ∈ K a class [J¹ᐟ²_a] with 2[J¹ᐟ²_a] = [J¹_m] maps to f_0g(a) in K^×/K^{×2} (Proposition 26), and a lemma on central extensions (Lemma 27, commutative up to sign) finishes it.
items.locator: Theorem 25, Proposition 26, Lemma 27 and proofs, pp.15–17, citing [6, §2.4, Theorem 9], [33, Lemma 2.4.5], [36, Lemma 2.8.2], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Cassels' descent map x − T
items.statement: x − T : J¹_m(K)/2J_m(K) → (L^×/L^{×2})_{N≡f_0} sends a non-Weierstrass point (x_0, 1, z_0) to x_0 − β, and a Weierstrass point to h_1(β) − h_0(β) (h_0 = t − x_0, h_1 = f(t, 1)/(t − x_0)). The induced map J¹(K)/2J(K) → (L^×/L^{×2}K^×)_{N≡f_0} is injective or 2-to-1 according as W[2] is trivial or not ([12]).
items.locator: Proof of Theorem 28, pp.18–19, citing [12], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Tau Ceti has the elliptic-curve analogue (TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/MordellWeil/SelmerGroup.lean), not this one. Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 28 (soluble SL_n(K)-orbits)
items.statement: For f of degree n = 2g + 2 with Δ(f), f_0 ≠ 0, soluble orbits for SL_n(K) (those whose regular pencil has F_m(K) ≠ ∅) with invariant form f exist iff C has a K-rational divisor of odd degree, and they are then in bijection with J¹_m(K)/2J_m(K). Proof: H¹(K, SL_n) = 1, so rational orbits are a torsor for H¹(K, J_m[2]), and [F(A_1, B_1)_m] = [F(A, B)_m] + j′(c) up to sign (8). For a point Q there is an explicit isotropic (g + 1)-plane; for a divisor of odd degree k, corestriction kills the order-4 class.
items.locator: Theorem 28 and proof, pp.18–19, arXiv:1310.7692v2 (error E1)
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 29 (soluble (SL_n/μ_2)(K)-orbits)
items.statement: Soluble orbits for (SL_n/μ_2)(K) (those with F(K) ≠ ∅) with invariant form f exist iff C has a K-rational divisor of odd degree. They are then in bijection with J¹(K)/2J(K), on which J(K)/2J(K) acts simply transitively. Absence without an odd-degree divisor uses 1 → T → X_m → X → 1 ([37, Corollary 3.22]).
items.locator: Theorem 29 and the preceding paragraph, pp.19–20, arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Orbits over finite fields (§7.1)
items.statement: Over F_q (q odd), with g(x) = ∏_{i≤m}g_i of degrees d_i, f always has an odd or even factorization. The number of (SL_n/μ_2)(F_q)-orbits with invariant form f is 2^m if all d_i are even and n ≡ 0 mod 4, 2^{m−1} if all d_i are even and n ≡ 2 mod 4, and 2^{m−2} otherwise. The stabilizers have the same sizes, so #{(A, B) : f_{A,B} = f} = |SL_n(F_q)|. By Lang's theorem every orbit is soluble.
items.note: The counts were rederived from Corollary 20. Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Orbits over R and C (§7.2)
items.statement: Over C there is one orbit. Over R, with 2m real roots: no orbits if f is negative definite; if f is positive definite, 2 orbits (n ≡ 0 mod 4) or 1 (n ≡ 2 mod 4), all soluble; if m > 0, 2^{2m−2} orbits (sign assignments to the real factors, modulo overall sign), of which 2^{m−1} are soluble. The stabilizer sizes are 2^{n/2}, 2^{n/2−1} and 2^{n/2+m−2} respectively.
items.note: The counts were rederived from Corollary 20. Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 30 (existence of rational orbits over a global field)
items.statement: Let K be a global field of characteristic ≠ 2 and C : z² = f with Div¹(C) locally soluble. Suppose J¹ has a locally soluble two-cover, i.e. W[2] is divisible by 2 in Sel_4(J/K). Then some (A, B) over K has invariant form f. Proof: with T = (Res_{K′/K}G_m)_{N=1}, the local-global principles for H¹(K, T) and H²(K, T), plus local injectivity of H¹(K_ν, T) → H¹(K_ν, J_m), show that [J¹_m] is divisible by 2.
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorems 31 and 14 and Lemma 32 (locally soluble orbits and Sel_2(J¹))
items.locator: Theorem 14, p.5; Theorem 31, Lemma 32 and proofs, pp.23–25, citing [4, Proposition 1], [28, Proposition 10.3], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: The Weil pairing on J[2] and J[4]
items.statement: The Weil pairings e_2 on J[2] and e_4 on J[4] are perfect and Galois-equivariant. The Selmer groups and the local Kummer images J(K_ν)/2J(K_ν), J(K_ν)/4J(K_ν) are isotropic for the induced cup-product pairings.
items.note: A3 plans torsion and pairings of abelian schemes. The isotropy of Kummer images (local Tate duality) is an ArithmeticGaloisDuality input.

items.name: Examples: locally soluble orbits without soluble orbits, and conversely
items.statement: For E : y² = x³ − 1221 (E(Q) = 0, Ш ≅ (Z/4)²), the quartic f = 3x⁴ − 12x³y + 11xy³ − 11y⁴ (Δ = −3⁵·11²·37²) has locally soluble orbits (from order-4 elements of Ш) but no soluble orbit. For f = −x⁴ + 2x³y + 104x²y² − 104xy³ − 2764y⁴ (Δ = −2⁸·571; L = Q(θ), θ⁴ − 2θ² + 2θ − 3 = 0, disc −2⁴·571, O_L = Z[θ], N(θ³ − θ) = −36), rational orbits exist but no locally soluble ones, since C is a nontrivial element of Ш(E)[2] = (Z/2)² not divisible by 2 in Sel_4. Here E is the conductor-571 curve y² + y = x³ − x² − 929x − 10595 (the paper prints y² + xy, E2).
items.note: Checked with PARI: disc(f) values, I = 0, J = 32967 (Jacobian y² = x³ − 3⁶·1221), analytic Ш of order 16 and 4, rank 0, conductor 571 and isomorphism to Jac(z² = f). Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Theorems 15 and 33 and Proposition 34 (integral representatives, κ = 4)
items.statement: For even n: if f has coefficients in 16Z (printed: 16^nZ, E4) and C : z² = f has locally soluble Div¹, then every locally soluble (SL_n/μ_2)(Q)-orbit with invariant form f has a representative in Z² ⊗ Sym²Z^n. Hence the orbits with disc(Ax − By) = 16f are in bijection with Sel_2(J¹) (Theorem 15, κ = 4). The proof reduces to Proposition 34, where 2^{4i} | f_0^{i−1}f_i. It works over Z_p with divisors D = Σ(P_i) − D* (m odd, m ≤ g + 1) and the explicit ideal I_D = ⟨f_0^{2m}R(f_0θ), P(f_0θ)I_f(n − 3 − m/2)⟩ with α = f_0^{2m}α_0. The norm is computed by a specialization argument over a generic ring.
items.locator: Theorem 15, p.5; Theorem 33, Proposition 34 and proofs, pp.25–28, citing [1, §2], [5, Proposition 8.2], [31, Proposition 2.9], [38, Lemma 3.8], arXiv:1310.7692v2 (misprints E4, E5)

items.name: Proposition 35 (uniqueness of integral representatives at good odd primes)
items.statement: For odd p, f ∈ Z_p[x, y] of even degree with p² ∤ Δ(f) and f_0 ≠ 0, and Div¹(C)(Q_p) ≠ ∅: the (SL_n/μ_2)(Z_p)-orbits with invariant form f are in bijection with the soluble (SL_n/μ_2)(Q_p)-orbits, and integral and rational stabilizers agree. Proof: R_f is maximal, the Néron model 𝒥 is fiberwise connected with 𝒥[2] ≅ (Res_{R/Z_p}μ_2)_{N=1}/μ_2, and 𝒥(Z_p)/2𝒥(Z_p) ≅ (R_f^×/R_f^{×2}Z_p^×)_{N≡1} ([31, Proposition 2.11]).
items.locator: Proposition 35 and proof, p.29, citing [10, §9.5 Theorem 1], [31], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.1 as a source.

items.name: Néron models: fiberwise connectedness
items.statement: If the special fiber of a proper regular model of a curve over Z_p is geometrically reduced and irreducible, the Néron model of its Jacobian is fiberwise connected, and 𝒥(Z_p) = J(Q_p) ([10, §9.5, Theorem 1]).
items.locator: Proof of Proposition 35, p.29, citing [10], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: R11.1 plans Néron models and their uniqueness.

items.name: Theorem 36 (counting irreducible G(Z)-orbits, after [1])
items.statement: For G = SL_n/μ_2 (n even), V(R) with Δ ≠ 0 and f not negative definite splits into components V^{(m,r)} (r ≤ 2^{2m−2} for m ≥ 1; 2 or 1 for m = 0 as n ≡ 0 or 2 mod 4). For a G(Z)-invariant S ⊂ V(Z)^{(m,r)} defined by finitely many congruence conditions, the number of G(Z)-classes of irreducible v ∈ S with H(v) < X is c_{m,r}∏_pν_p(S)X^{n+1} + o(X^{n+1}), with c_{m,r} the volume of a fundamental domain of height < 1 ([1, Theorems 9 and 17]).
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.2 as a source.

items.name: Definitions 37 and 39 (functions defined by congruence conditions; large families)
items.statement: φ : U(Z) → [0, 1] is defined by congruence conditions if φ = ∏_pφ_p with φ_p locally constant outside a measure-zero closed set and ∫φ_p ≠ 0. A set F of integral binary n-ic forms is large if it is defined by congruence conditions and, for almost all p, its complement mod p lies in S_0(F_p) for a fixed subscheme S_0 of codimension ≥ 2. The forms with locally soluble Div¹, and those with locally soluble C, are large ([26, Lemma 15]).
items.locator: Definitions 37 and 39 and the following paragraph, pp.30–31, citing [26, Lemma 15], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.2 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 38 (weighted orbit counts)
items.statement: If φ : V(Z) → [0, 1] is G(Z)-invariant and defined by congruence conditions, and S ⊂ V(Z)^{(m,r)} is defined by congruence conditions, then the weighted count of G(Z)-classes of irreducible v ∈ S of height < X is ≤ c_{m,r}X^{n+1}∏_p∫φ_p + o(X^{n+1}). This follows by sifting from Theorem 36, as in [7, §2.7].
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.2 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 42 (tail estimate via the geometric sieve)
items.statement: For a large family F with p-adic closures F_p and any M > 0, #⋃_{p>M}{f ∈ I(m) : f ∉ F_p, H(f) < X} = O(X^{n+1}/M) + O(X^n), by Bhargava's quantitative Ekedahl sieve ([2, Theorem 3.3]), since the conditions are codimension ≥ 2 mod p. With a sifting argument this gives #{C ∈ F : H(C) < X} = Σ_mμ_∞({f ∈ I(m) : H < X})∏_pμ_p(F_p) + o(X^{n+1}) (22).
items.locator: Proposition 42 and (22), p.33, citing [2, Theorem 3.3], [7, §2.7], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: The geometric sieve is also an item of PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-22 (ST.2); coalesce. Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.2 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 40 (Sel_2(J¹) as a weighted orbit count)
items.statement: For a large F contained in the forms with locally soluble Div¹, with coefficients in 16Z (printed 16^nZ, E4): Σ_{C∈F, H<X}#Sel_2(J¹) ≤ Σ_mΣ_{r soluble}N_w(V(Z)^{(m,r)}_F; X) + o(X^{n+1}) (18). The weight w(v) = (Σ_{v′}#Stab_{G(Q)}(v′)/#Stab_{G(Z)}(v′))^{−1} (17) counts each G(Q)-class once, up to the ≤ 2^{2g} stabilizer and negligibly many nontrivial stabilizers ([1, Proposition 14]); it is a product of local weights as in [7, Proposition 3.6].
items.locator: Theorem 40, (17)–(20) and proof, pp.31–32, citing [1], [7], arXiv:1310.7692v2 (misprint E4)
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Local masses and the product formula
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: The Tamagawa number τ(SL_n/μ_2) = 2
items.statement: The Tamagawa number of G = SL_n/μ_2 is 2.
items.note: AdelicAlgebraicGroups AA.2 constructs Tamagawa measures but leaves individual values out of scope. Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 41 (the upper bound for Σ#Sel_2(J¹))
items.statement: For F as in Theorem 40: Σ_{C∈F, H(C)<X}#Sel_2(J¹) ≤ Σ_mτ(G)μ_∞({f ∈ I(m) : H(f) < X})∏_pμ_p(F_p) + o(X^{n+1}) (21), with τ(G) = 2. Dividing by (22) proves Theorem 6.
items.locator: Theorem 41, (21), p.33; proof of Theorem 6, p.33, arXiv:1310.7692v2 (misprint E4)
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Definition 43 (admissible families)
items.statement: A set F of integral binary n-ic forms is admissible if it is defined by congruence conditions and, for all large p, its p-adic closure contains every f over Z_p for which z² = f(x, y) has a Q_p-point.
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 44 (general version of Theorem 1)
items.statement: Let F be a large family of integral binary forms of degree 2g + 2, and p, q primes neither of which is a square modulo the other. Suppose that for a positive proportion of f ∈ F: f, pf, qf, pqf all lie in F and have points over Q_p and Q_q; J has split semistable reduction of toric dimension 1 at p and good reduction at q; and, if 2 has a unique prime above it in Q(√p, √q), the corresponding conditions hold at 2 (added, E3). Then for a positive proportion of f ∈ F, J¹(Q) = ∅ and Sel_2(J¹) = ∅.
items.note: Stated without proof. Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorems A.1–A.2 (odd and even 2-Selmer ranks occur with positive proportion)
items.statement: In the family y² = a_nx^n + ⋯ + a_0 (n ≥ 3) over Q ordered by height, both odd and even 2^∞-Selmer ranks occur with proportion ≥ 2^{−4n−4}; assuming finiteness of Ш[2^∞], so do odd and even Mordell–Weil ranks (Theorem A.1). Over any number field, in the full family or any admissible family, a positive proportion have even and a positive proportion odd 2-Selmer rank, and likewise for the 2^∞-Selmer rank (Theorem A.2).
items.locator: Appendix A, Theorems A.1–A.2, p.35; proofs pp.36–37, arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: The constant 2^{−4n−4} was rederived: the quadruples {±f, ±2f} for f in the congruence class of Proposition A.4 with H(f) < X/2 are disjoint. Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem A.3 (parity of 2-Selmer ranks in a biquadratic family of twists)
items.statement: Let F = K(√α, √β) be biquadratic with some prime p_0 of K having a unique prime above it in F, and let C/K have Jacobian J. Suppose C(K_{p_0}) ≠ ∅ and J has split semistable reduction of toric dimension 1 at p_0, and that C(K_p) ≠ ∅ and J has good reduction at every other p with a unique prime above it in F. Then rk_{2^∞}(J) + rk_{2^∞}(J^α) + rk_{2^∞}(J^β) + rk_{2^∞}(J^{αβ}) ≡ 1 mod 2. If also C^α, C^β, C^{αβ} have points at all such p, the same holds for 2-Selmer ranks.
items.locator: Theorem A.3, p.36; proof pp.38–39, arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Proposition A.4 and Lemma A.5 (families with the required local behaviour)
items.statement: If a_2 ≡ 1, a_{2g+1} ≡ 4 and all other a_i ≡ 0 mod 8, then y² = f(x) reduces (after y ↦ 2y + x) to y² + xy = x^{2g+1} with one split node, so J has split toric reduction of dimension 1 at 2 and C(Q_2) ≠ ∅. Hence among y² = ±f, ±2f both parities occur (Proposition A.4). For p odd (Lemma A.5): squarefree f̄ with an F_q-root gives good reduction and points on all twists; f̄ = (x − a)²h with h squarefree, h(a) ∈ F_q^{×2} and an F_q-root gives split toric reduction of dimension 1; and if f̄ is not λh² and q > 4n², then C(K) ≠ ∅.
items.locator: Proposition A.4, Lemma A.5 and proofs, pp.36–37, citing [26, Lemma 15], arXiv:1310.7692v2 (misprint E5)
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem A.7 and Corollary A.8 (Brauer relations and 2^∞-Selmer parity)
items.statement: For a principally polarized abelian variety A/K, a Galois extension F/K with group G and a Brauer relation Θ = Σn_iH_i: Σ_{ρ∈S_Θ}m_ρ ≡ ord_p∏_i(c̃_{A/F^{H_i}}·|Ш^{[p]}_{A/F^{H_i}}|) mod 2, where m_ρ are multiplicities in the dual p^∞-Selmer group and S_Θ the self-dual representations with odd regulator constant ([17, Theorem 1.6], with the Ш[2] term for p = 2). For F = K(√α, √β) and Θ = {1} − C_2^a − C_2^b − C_2^c + 2G, S_Θ = {1, ε_a, ε_b, ε_c}, which gives the formula (†) for the four twists.
items.locator: Theorem A.7, Corollary A.8 and proofs, pp.38–39, citing [17], [18], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

items.name: Poonen–Stoll: the parity of Ш[2] is a sum of local terms
items.statement: For a principally polarized Jacobian, the parity of ord_2|Ш^{[2]}| is a sum of local terms, 1 or 0 according as Pic^{g−1}(C) is empty or not over the completion ([26, §8]).
items.locator: Proof of Theorem A.3, p.39, citing [26, §8], arXiv:1310.7692v2
items.note: Routed to ArithmeticStatistics ST.4 as a source.

routes.reason: ST.2 owns the uniform orbit counts and the tail estimates that pass to infinitely many local conditions: the congruence-weighted count of irreducible orbits (Theorems 36 and 38), large families, and the geometric-sieve tail (Proposition 42).

ST.4 owns Bhargava–Shankar Selmer averages and their statistical consequences, using ST.1's orbit-to-Selmer comparison. That covers the average of #Sel_2(J¹) (Theorems 6, 40 and 41 with the local masses and τ(SL_n/μ_2) = 2) and its consequences (Theorems 1, 2, 5, 7 and 12, Corollaries 3 and 8, Remark 4, Theorem 44). It also covers the Dokchitsers' appendix, which supplies the Selmer-parity input: odd and even 2-Selmer ranks with positive proportion via Brauer relations, regulator constants and the Poonen–Stoll local terms.

RP.1 owns Kummer maps, finite Selmer groups and descent. Two-covers of torsors, the class W[2] with its odd-factorization description, and the 2-Selmer sets Sel_2(J¹) and those of order k are descent objects. RP.3 owns torsor descent and its comparison with the Brauer–Manin obstruction, where the Hasse-principle failures for J¹ and Sym^k(C) belong (Corollary 9, Theorems 10–11); the Skorobogatov–Stoll comparison itself is planned there.

R11.4 owns the degree-zero Picard schemes and generalized Jacobians of semistable curves. That covers the nodal curve C_m with generalized Jacobian J_m, the sequence 0 → T → J_m → J → 0, and the description of J_m[2], J[2] and the torsors W_m[2], W[2] by factors of f.
SF.3 owns divisors, line bundles and Picard objects. The comparison of rational divisor classes with rational divisors, via Pic_{C/K}(K)/Pic(C/K) ↪ Br(K′/K), is a Picard-object statement.

review.reason: Confirmed. Theorem 44 on pp.34–35 imposes local conditions only at p and q, while the only proof available is Theorem A.3 (p.36), which requires C(K_p) ≠ ∅ and good reduction at every p ≠ p_0 with a unique prime above it in F, and, for the 2-Selmer conclusion, points on all four twists at every such p. For F = Q(√p, √q) the primes with a unique prime above them are p and q — which is what the non-residue hypothesis buys — and 2 exactly when 2 ramifies in one quadratic subfield and is inert in another, that is when one of p, q is ≡ 3 mod 4 and the other ≡ 5 mod 8; (p,q) = (5,3) satisfies both that and the non-residue hypothesis, since (5/3) = (3/5) = −1. No other prime can have a unique prime above it, because an unramified decomposition group in a Klein four extension is cyclic of order at most 2. Both stated alternatives also work: for p ≡ q ≡ 1 mod 4 the prime 2 is unramified in F and so has at least two primes above it, and if the prime that is ≡ 1 mod 4 is ≡ 1 mod 8 then 2 splits in that quadratic subfield and the decomposition group again has order at most 2. Theorem 44 carries no proof of its own in the paper, so the missing hypothesis is a gap in a stated result, as recorded.

Theorem 15 on p.5 claims κ = 4, that is κ² = 16; with 16^n the same argument would give κ = 4^n. So the printed hypothesis is an unnecessarily strong misprint that the proof does not use.

review.reason: Confirmed, all four. The p.26 display prints 'g(x,y) = x^n + f_1x^{n−1}y + f_0f_2x^{n−2}y + ⋯ + f_0^{n−1}f_ny^n', where the third term needs y² for homogeneity: with y² one has g(f_0x, y) = f_0^{n−1}f(x,y), which is the identity the proof then uses. The p.37 sentence prints '> n rational points', while the points to be avoided — those whose x-coordinate is a root of f, plus the points at infinity — number up to 2n + 2, so '> n' does not by itself produce a good point. The two reference slips are printed as quoted on pp.41–42: Skorobogatov's Torsors and rational points is Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics 144 (2001), not 114 (2007), and Algebra & Number Theory volume 1 is 2007, not 1997.
